text.p: The ordinary, everyday credit card is on its way to becoming a sophisticated tool that in a few years may significantly re-shape business travel.
-- A traveller making a hotel, rental car or airline reservation over the Internet sticks a card in a slot in a laptop or desktop computer, and the reservation is instantly downloaded into the card.
-- On arriving at the airport gate, car rental counter or hotel lobby, the same card is swiped through an electronic reading slot and out comes a boarding pass, car keys or a hotel room card key.
-- Mileage points and other frequent traveller reward credit is recorded on the card, where it is available for upgrades and other uses.

That scenario is from Steve Norman, vice president of electronic travel marketing at American Express. His company and others in the travel industry are working to bring the so-called "smart card" into working reality.
A credit card with a sophisticated computer chip embedded in it, such cards are capable of carrying and receiving far more information than current cards with just magnetic stripes on them.

In the next few weeks a group of employes from American Express and from IBM will begin using fully functional smart cards to test how they work for air travel. The test will be run through electronic boarding devices American Airlines has installed at 21 U.S. airports.

The boarding systems allow customers with reservations but without checked luggage to go directly to a gate and get a boarding pass with seat assignemnt by running the card through the device. Because of current security measures, the customers will also be asked for a photo identification.

An American spokesman said that carrier is working on an enhancement for the electronic gate that could allow many passengers to use the devices without displaying a photo identification. It might employ profiles developed by the FBI to screen out high-risk passengers or other technology.
What the industry is working for in the long run, according to Norman, is to smooth out the travel process.
"One thing this can do is dramatically reduce the amount of time you spend in line ... at the airport, the hotel, the car rental counter," he said.
"What's your seeing is a number of companies trying new things all with the same objective -- to increase customer loyalty (to brands) and reduce time spent in line," he added.
On another travel front, the pressure to hold down expenses comes through in a poll Frequent Flyer magazine took of nearly 9,000 readers.
Fifth-nine perent said they had spent a Saturday night out of town in order to reap the benefits of lower air fares that such stay-overs usually offer.
In addition, nearly half of the travelers who responded said they were taking fewer last-minute trips in order to avoid the high prices of spot market airline tickets.

Another industry trend -- crowded hotels -- also showed up in the survey with 74 percent of those replying saying they had been unable to book a room in the hotel of their first choice during the past year.
The complete reader survey covering dozens of issues is available in the magazine's December issue.
